messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rana Haddad was 38 when she came for treatment, a divorced middle school principal who had built a reputation for composure and decisiveness, and who now found herself frightened by how little steadiness she felt inside. She had served in combat years earlier, and when she spoke about the event that continued to grip her, the account came out in jagged pieces rather than a clean story. She remembered being in an armored vehicle moving through a narrow urban street, then shouting over the radio, then the crack of gunfire and a concussive blast that seemed to swallow the rest. What came back most forcefully was not a sequence but fragments: the metallic pop of rounds hitting nearby, someone yelling for cover, the high-pitched whine in her ears after the explosion. When those memories surfaced now, she did not simply “think about it”; she heard those sounds in her head as if they were happening again, and with them came a surge of rage so strong it startled her.

Over time, the broken, sensory nature of the memory came to mean something corrosive to Rana. Because she could not put the event in the right order, she had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with the way she had handled it and with the way she was handling herself now. She was certain that a stronger person would be able to tell the story straight, would not still be ambushed by sounds from years ago, would not feel this much fury on recall. The memory fragments also fed a broader bitterness: if the worst moments of her life could reduce people to noise, confusion, and survival, then what exactly was solid or worthwhile anymore? In session she said, with flat conviction, that nothing in her life felt meaningful now. She also carried a settled mistrust of other people, as if the world exposed in that event had shown her too clearly that people could not be relied on.

That way of seeing things kept her body and attention organized around danger. Rana said she felt on guard even inside her own home. She checked locks repeatedly, noted where she would exit each room, and did not feel fully at ease anywhere until she had identified an escape route. At school, this had become woven into her day. As principal, she scanned hallways, positioned herself near doors during meetings, and silently calculated how she would move students and staff out of the building if something happened. Her mistrust sharpened this vigilance; she did not assume other adults would notice trouble or respond well, so she believed she had to stay alert for everyone. Her conviction that she was a “lousy coper” made the vigilance feel even more necessary: if she was already failing internally, she told herself, she could not afford to let her guard down externally.

Living in that state of readiness made the memories easier to set off. A slammed locker, a burst of static over the school intercom, students shouting in a crowded corridor could pull her back before she understood what was happening. The more intensely she monitored for threat, the more quickly her mind filled with the old sounds—the yelling, the radio traffic, the blast—and the more the memory returned in the same disordered fragments. At home, being on edge in her own living room meant that a noise outside or a neighbor’s raised voice could leave her hearing combat sounds in her head. She would then feel the same hot rage rise in her chest, with no clear place to put it.

Those episodes deepened what she believed about herself and about the world. Each time she found herself mapping exits at a parent conference or sitting rigidly through the evening in her own house, she took it as further proof that something in her had been permanently damaged. The fact that she could not relax where she lived and worked made her think her life had narrowed into mere survival, which reinforced the sense that it no longer held meaning. Her constant watchfulness also sustained her mistrust; if she was always scanning for what could go wrong, other people appeared less like sources of support than potential liabilities.

By the time Rana sought help, the strain had become hard to hide. Staff had begun to notice how tense she was during routine announcements and drills, and she hated what it meant to feel herself rehearsing exits during meetings with teachers and parents. She came in after a recent intercom burst sent her into a flood of sound and anger so abruptly that she had to close her office door and sit alone until she could speak calmly again. What frightened her most was not only the return of the memory, but the possibility that this was all she would be from now on: a woman who could not trust, could not settle, and could not make sense of what had happened well enough to reclaim a meaningful life. What she wanted, carefully and almost skeptically, was to believe that her mind was not beyond repair.
